# Learning Objectives CP: ANOVA

 - Perform one-way and two-way ANOVA including interactions
 - Interpret results of an ANOVA
 - Understand components of the ANOVA table
 - Check assumptions of an ANOVA
 - Be able to perform Post-Hoc testing

# Introduction

Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is an effective treatment in a variety of diagnoses, and is investigated intensively in the LUMC. One research line concerns injection of CD34+-cells from a donor in patients with, for instance, leukemia. CD34 is a surface marker for  hematopoietic progenitor cells which can differentiate into a variety of lymphoid and myeloid hematopoietic cells. The efficacy of such an injection can be evaluated by measuring CD19+ cells in bone marrow which represent newly differentiated B-cells. CD19 is a cell-surface protein present on normal and neoplastic B-cells. 

In a biomedical experiment the goal is to evaluate (1) the dose-effect relationship between injection of CD34+ cells and the engraftment, as measured by the concentration of CD19+ cells, and (2) the difference in dose-effect between injecting CD34+ cells from umbilical cord blood (UCB), bone marrow (BM) or mobilized peripheral blood (mPB). A number of mice were injected with varying doses of CD34+ cells from UCB, BM or mPB, and in each animal the engraftment was evaluated by measuring the concentration CD19+ cells in bone marrow of these animals.

## Q7: Post-hoc analysis

Perform a post-hoc analysis for factor dose. A post-hoc analysis identifies which particular levels of a factor actually differ from each other. This can be done by performing pair-wise t-tests. To simplify the analysis, we first create a new column with the square root (or log) transformed values (pick your choice).

```{r}
  data$cd19t <- sqrt(data$cd19)
  data$cd19t <- log(data$cd19)
```

A t-test can then be performed as follows:
```{r}
  t.test(data$cd19t[data$dose == '0.10'], data$cd19t[data$dose == '0.5'])
```

The `with` function allows to use columns of a data frame as if they were variables. The same line from above can be evaluated as:

```{r}
  with(data, t.test(cd19t[dose == '0.10'], cd19t[dose == '0.5']))
```

Perform all pair-wise comparisons between dosage levels using t-tests by repeating the line above (for the square root transformation).

**fillin**:

# Learning R

At the beginning of the exercise, you had to find out which columns of the `cd19` data set were factors by consulting the data dictionary. Here, we introduce functions `sapply` and `lapply` that allow to determine these levels automatically.

The R-function `sapply` can be used to apply a function to all elements of a list or vector one-by-one. The following code determines the types of the columns in the data set. Note, that a `data.frame` in R is a list of its columns, so that, for example, column 1 can be accessed as `data[[1]]`. Function `class` returns the type of an R object (list/vector/etc.).

```{r}
  colTypes <- c(class(data[[1]]), class(data[[2]]), class(data[[3]]))
```

The same can be achieved with the `sapply` function.

```{r}
  colTypes <- sapply(data, class)
```

This code will work for any data frame and is not limited to three columns. Note, that for `sapply` also the column names are retained. R can annotate each element of a vector with a name which does not play a role in data manipulation but increases readability.

`lapply` is very similar to `sapply`. It returns a `list` and can therefore construct more complex return values (for example the differnt levels per column).

The function `which` converts a logical vector (a vector containing TRUE/FALSE values) into the positions where a TRUE value is found.

`lapply` and `which` are combined to list the factor levels of all factors in a data set. Use an LLM to get a detailed explanation of the code.

```{r}
  lapply(which(sapply(data, class) == 'factor'), function(i)levels(data[[i]]))
```
